how-many-unused-saas-seats-am-i-paying-f.text:
← SaaS seat true-up calculator

How many unused SaaS seats am I paying for?

Most SaaS renewals auto-renew the seat count from the last term, not the seat count actually in use. The gap between purchased and used seats is money spent every month whether anyone logs in or not — and it's the single most concrete number to bring into a renewal negotiation.

Open the free SaaS seat true-up calculator

What a renewal invoice does not show

Purchased is not used. A vendor's invoice bills the seat count on the contract, not the seat count logged into last week — the gap between the two is invisible until someone runs the audit.

Avoidable spend compounds by term. A monthly per-seat waste figure looks small; multiplied by the months remaining on the current term, and again by a full year, it's the number that actually changes a negotiating position.

Overage cuts the other way too. A team that has grown past its purchased seat count is paying overage, sometimes at a contracted premium above list price — a mismatch worth catching before the invoice does.

A number you can defend

  1. Enter seats purchased and seats actually used in your latest access review.
  2. Enter the per-seat monthly price and the months remaining in the current term.
  3. If seats used exceed seats purchased, enter any contracted overage premium above list price (0% if it bills at the same rate).
  4. Read unused seats, utilization percentage, and avoidable spend for the month, the remaining term, and the full year.

Worked example

20 seats purchased, 14 seats used in the latest review, at $18 per seat per month, with 4 months remaining in the term: that's 6 unused seats and 70% utilization. Monthly avoidable spend is $108. Through the 4 remaining months of the term, that's $432 in avoidable spend. If the renewal goes through at the same seat count for a full year, it's $1,296 that a seat reduction to 14 would release.

Common questions

How many unused SaaS seats am I paying for?

Unused seats are purchased seats minus seats used in your latest review. Buying 20 seats and finding 14 actively used in your last audit means 6 unused seats and 70% utilization — a number worth having in hand before the renewal conversation starts.

How much could I save by right-sizing before renewal?

Monthly avoidable spend is unused seats multiplied by the price per seat. 6 unused seats at $18 each is $108 a month, $432 through a 4-month remaining term, and $1,296 over a full year if the seat count is never adjusted at renewal.

What if I'm actually over my purchased seat count instead of under it?

Seats used above the purchased count become overage, billed at list price plus any contracted overage premium you enter — 0% keeps the same per-seat price as a default. The calculator reports extra annual spend from the overage the same way it reports avoidable spend from unused seats, so either direction of mismatch has a dollar figure attached.

Renewal prep for SaaS operators

Stop renewing seats nobody uses.

Enter the seats you bought, the seats people actually use, and the per-seat price. Get a private, defensible estimate of avoidable subscription spend before your next renewal conversation.

How many unused SaaS seats am I paying for? · vs. Zylo · vs. Vendr · vs. a spreadsheet

Plan details

Leave at 0% when extra seats bill at the same price. Enter the contracted premium when the vendor charges more for unpurchased seats.

Some contracts will not let you renew below a minimum seat count. Enter it here so the avoidable figures reflect what you can actually drop, not the full unused count.

Many contracts require written notice before renewal to cut seats, or it auto-renews at the full count. Enter the renewal date and that notice window and the tool will say whether there is still time to act.

Your review

6unused seats
70%seat utilization
$108.00avoidable per month
$432.00avoidable through renewal
A seat review could release $1,296.00 over a full year if the unused seats are not renewed.

Common questions

What counts as a “used” seat?

Whatever your own review decides, and the definition is the whole game. A seat assigned to someone who left, a seat held for a contractor whose project ended, a seat that has not seen a login in ninety days — all of them are provisioned and billed, and none of them are used in any sense your finance team would recognise. Most vendor admin consoles will export last-login per user; that export, not the assigned-seat count, is the number to type here.

Why does it show both a remaining-term figure and an annual one?

Because they answer different questions. The remaining-term figure is what the current contract still commits you to — on the worked example, 6 unused seats at $18 with 4 months left is $432 you are going to pay regardless. The annual figure, $1,296, is what those same seats cost if you renew at the same count. The first is usually sunk; the second is the one you can actually act on, and it is why a seat review is worth doing before the renewal conversation rather than after it.

What if we are over the purchased count instead of under?

Then the tool prices the overage rather than the saving, and that is often the more urgent number. Overage is commonly billed at list plus a contracted premium, so there is a field for that premium — leave it at 0% if your agreement charges plain list. Being over is not necessarily bad; it can mean the product is working. It just should not be a surprise on the true-up invoice.

Does this tell me what to do at renewal?

No. It sizes the number so you can decide, and a contracted seat minimum — enter it in the field above — is already subtracted from what counts as droppable, so it will not tell you to cut below a floor your agreement enforces. It still cannot see step pricing: dropping from 20 to 14 may not save what the per-seat math implies if it crosses a volume pricing tier, and a seat released today may have to be re-bought at a worse rate in six months. Read your own agreement for true-up timing and whether reductions are permitted mid-term at all — many contracts allow additions any time and reductions only at renewal.

What does the contract seat minimum field do?

It caps how many of the unused seats the tool treats as actually droppable. Some agreements will not let the seat count fall below a floor at renewal no matter how low usage is — enter that floor and the avoidable figures shrink to match what you can really cut. On 20 purchased, 14 used, and a 17-seat minimum, the tool still reports 6 unused seats but only 3 as droppable, because the other 3 are locked in by the minimum regardless of usage. Leave it at 0 if your agreement has no floor.

Can I use this across several tools at once?

Run them one at a time and add up the annual figures. Each subscription has its own price, term, and overage treatment, so averaging them together hides the one that matters. In practice a handful of tools usually account for most of the waste, and doing them individually is what makes that visible.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No account and no network requests — the calculation runs entirely in your browser. A saved scenario stores only the totals you typed and stays in this browser; reset deletes it. The shareable link carries the same totals in the URL itself, so a scenario is only shared with whoever you send that link to — nothing is uploaded to a server to make the link work. There are no cookies and no analytics vendors, and the anonymous feature counter is local and can be turned off below. Seat counts and prices are commercially sensitive, which is exactly why none of this leaves the page.

Why does it ask for a renewal date and a notice period?

Because a seat reduction usually cannot happen just because usage is low — most contracts allow it only at renewal, and many require written notice a set number of days before that renewal or the agreement auto-renews at the full purchased count regardless of usage. Enter the renewal date and that notice window (leave both blank if you don’t know or your agreement has none) and the tool checks whether the deadline has already passed. If it has, the saving above is not avoidable this cycle — it tells you that plainly instead of showing a number you cannot actually act on, and estimates when the next window opens assuming an annual term.

vs-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← SaaS Seat True-Up Calculator

This calculator vs. a spreadsheet

A lot of SaaS operators already track renewals in a spreadsheet: one column for purchased seats, one for seats actually used, a formula that subtracts them and multiplies by price. That arithmetic is trivial and a spreadsheet does it fine. What it does not do on its own is check whether every one of those unused seats can actually be dropped -- a contracted seat minimum can force you to keep paying for some of them no matter how few people log in, and it does not check whether there is still time to act -- most seat contracts gate a reduction behind a written-notice deadline, and a subtraction says nothing about whether that window is still open.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What's purchased seats minus used seats, times price? Either one — a spreadsheet subtracts and multiplies fine.
Does a contracted seat minimum stop some of that "unused" total from actually being droppable? This calculator — it nets the minimum against usage automatically; a spreadsheet needs you to build that check in yourself.
Has the written-notice deadline for this renewal already passed? This calculator — checks the renewal date against the notice period and tells you directly; a plain seat-count cell has no date logic at all.
Is the saving figure still avoidable this cycle, or did the window already close? This calculator — states it plainly instead of leaving a stale-looking number for you to reinterpret.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere? No, on either — but this calculator needs no account, no template, and no formula to maintain.
Run a seat true-up now

This tool needs no account and nothing installed: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and the seat counts, price, and renewal date you enter stay on this device — nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Isn't unused SaaS spend just purchased seats minus used seats, times price?

That subtraction is trivial and a spreadsheet does it fine. What it does not do on its own is check whether every one of those unused seats can actually be dropped: a contracted seat minimum can force you to keep paying for some of them regardless of how few people log in, and a plain subtraction has no way to know your contract carries one unless you remember to build that check in yourself.

Why does the renewal notice deadline matter if the seat count is already unused?

Most seat contracts do not let you reduce at will — the reduction has to be submitted by a written-notice deadline before the term ends, or the renewal auto-renews at the full purchased count regardless of usage. A spreadsheet cell showing an unused-seat saving says nothing about whether that window is still open. This calculator checks the renewal date against the notice period and tells you directly whether the saving is still avoidable this cycle, due soon, or already lost.

What happens if my spreadsheet has a stale seat count in it?

Nothing catches it — a spreadsheet keeps reporting whatever number is in the cell, whether it reflects this renewal or one from two quarters ago. This calculator takes the counts you type for this review, so nothing carries over silently from a previous session, and it does not save what you type once you leave the page.

Does this replace a company's own SaaS spend tracker?

No. A spreadsheet or procurement system that tracks every subscription, every renewal date, and every seat count across the whole SaaS portfolio is still the right tool for that ongoing record. This page answers one question at a time — of the seats on this one renewal, how many are avoidable, and is there still time to act — and nothing it computes is saved anywhere once you leave the page.

vs-vendr.html.text:
← SaaS Seat True-Up Calculator

This calculator vs. Vendr

Vendr is a well-known SaaS buying platform, described on vendr.com as software purchasing and renewal management backed by a team of buyers and pricing data gathered across its customer base. Bring it a renewal and its buyers negotiate directly with the vendor on your behalf, aiming to land a lower price than you would get alone, and it can also carry the procurement paperwork for the deal. Pricing is by quote, and using it means engaging Vendr's team to run a negotiation, not opening a page and typing numbers.

That makes Vendr the right choice for one job: having someone else negotiate a lower price on a SaaS renewal. This page does not do that job, and does not try to. It negotiates with no one, contacts no vendor, and has no pricing data from other customers — it takes the seat counts and price you already have for one renewal and tells you how much of that price is unused seats, which is a number worth knowing whether or not anyone ever negotiates the price itself.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Can someone negotiate a lower per-seat price on this renewal for me? Vendr or a comparable buying platform — that is a negotiation this page cannot do.
Of the seats I am about to pay for at whatever price is quoted, how many are actually unused? This calculator — type purchased seats, seats used, price, and months left; get the avoidable spend in seconds, no signup.
Do I want Vendr's negotiators or procurement team handling the purchase paperwork? Vendr or a comparable platform — this page has no negotiators and touches no paperwork.
Is it worth even starting a renegotiation, or would trimming unused seats alone cover the overage? This calculator's numbers first — knowing the unused-seat cost is a reasonable input to that decision, negotiated price or not.

Nothing stops these two from being used together: a true-up here can be the number you bring into a Vendr negotiation, or the reason a negotiation is not needed at all because trimming seats already closes the gap. This calculator is deliberately the opposite shape from a buying platform: nothing to engage, no fee, and nothing you type ever leaves your browser. That makes it useful for sizing the unused-seat cost on a renewal you already have numbers for, and the wrong tool for having someone negotiate the vendor down — that is exactly the job a platform like Vendr is built for.

It needs no account, no negotiator, and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or a platform like Vendr?

They do different jobs. Vendr is a paid SaaS buying platform, described on Vendr's own site at vendr.com, that negotiates software purchases and renewals on a customer's behalf — its team of buyers uses market pricing data gathered across its customer base to push a vendor toward a lower price, and it can also front the paperwork and procurement workflow for the purchase. That is a negotiation service: someone else's buyers talk to the vendor for you, typically as part of a paid plan or a percentage-of-savings fee. This page does not negotiate anything and does not talk to any vendor. It has no market pricing data and no buyers — it takes the renewal quote already in front of you (purchased seats, seats actually used, price, months left) and turns it into an avoidable-spend figure in your browser, right now, with no signup and nothing sent anywhere.

Is this page affiliated with Vendr?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Vendr. Vendr is named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not, based on Vendr's own public site.

vs-zylo.html.text:
← SaaS Seat True-Up Calculator

This calculator vs. Zylo

Zylo is a well-known enterprise SaaS spend management platform, described on zylo.com as continuous discovery and control over an organization's software portfolio. It works by connecting to financial systems — ERP, accounts payable, and expense platforms — and to SSO providers, so it can find every SaaS application an organization is paying for, not just the ones someone remembers to list. Pricing is by quote rather than published on the site, and buying it means becoming a customer of an ongoing platform, not opening a page.

That makes Zylo the right choice for one job: continuously discovering and governing an entire, possibly unknown, SaaS portfolio across an organization. This page does not do that job, and does not try to. It has no integrations, connects to nothing, and does not discover anything — it takes the numbers you already have for one renewal and turns them into an avoidable-spend figure.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What SaaS tools is my organization even paying for? Zylo or a comparable discovery platform — that requires connecting financial and SSO data this page never sees.
How many of the seats on this one renewal I already have a quote for are unused? This calculator — type purchased seats, seats used, price, and months left; get the avoidable spend in seconds, no signup.
Do I need ongoing, cross-portfolio spend governance and renewal alerts for every app in the company? Zylo or a comparable platform — this page remembers nothing between renewals and tracks nothing across tools.
Is this quoted overage premium going to cost more than staying at the purchased seat count? This calculator's overage field, next to the same renewal numbers.

This calculator is deliberately the opposite shape from a spend management platform: nothing to connect, nothing billed monthly, and nothing you type ever leaves your browser. That makes it useful for a single upcoming renewal you already have numbers for, and the wrong tool for finding SaaS spend you do not already know about across an entire organization — that is exactly the job a platform like Zylo is built for.

It needs no account, no integration, and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or a platform like Zylo?

They answer different questions. Zylo is a paid, ongoing enterprise platform built to discover your organization's entire SaaS portfolio by connecting to financial systems (ERP, accounts payable, expense) and SSO providers, then track spend and utilization across every application it finds — described on Zylo's own site at zylo.com. That is a data-integration project: connecting live feeds, standing up a system of record, and paying for it on an ongoing quoted contract. This page does not do that job, and does not try to. It has no integrations, discovers nothing on its own, and does not know your SaaS portfolio exists. What it does is take the one renewal you already have in front of you — purchased seats, seats actually used, price, months left — and turn it into an avoidable-spend figure in your browser, right now, with no signup and nothing connected.

Is this page affiliated with Zylo?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Zylo. Zylo is named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not, based on Zylo's own public site.
